en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes, 4.
The Training Rule on Old Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the former wife of the Venerable Udāyī had gone forth among the bhikkhunīs.
She used to come frequently into the presence of the Venerable Udāyī,
and the Venerable Udāyī also used to go frequently into her presence.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was having his meal dispensed by that bhikkhunī.

Then, in the morning, the Venerable Udāyī dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached that bhikkhunī. Having approached, he sat down on a seat while exposing his private parts in front of that bhikkhunī.
That bhikkhunī also sat down on a seat while exposing her private parts in front of the Venerable Udāyī.
Then the Venerable Udāyī, being lustful, gazed intently at that bhikkhunī’s private parts. His semen was discharged.
Then the Venerable Udāyī said to that bhikkhunī:
“Go, sister, bring some water; I will wash my inner robe.”
“Noble sir, I myself will wash it,” she said;
then she took a portion of that impurity with her mouth and placed another portion into her womb.
By means of that, she conceived a fetus.
The bhikkhunīs said, “This bhikkhunī is unchaste; she is pregnant.
She informed the bhikkhunīs of this matter, saying, “Venerable ladies, I am not unchaste.”
The bhikkhunīs complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the venerable Udāyī have an old robe washed for a bhikkhunī?
Then those bhikkhunīs informed the bhikkhus of this matter.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the Venerable Udāyī have an old robe washed for a bhikkhunī?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, Udāyi, that you had an old robe washed for a bhikkhunī?
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Is she a relative of yours, Udāyi, or not a relative?”
“‘She is unrelated to me, Blessed One.
‘Foolish man, one who is unrelated does not know whether [an act] is appropriate or inappropriate, inspiring or uninspiring.
Yet you, foolish man, have had an unrelated bhikkhunī wash an old robe for you!’”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘If any monk should have an unrelated nun wash, dye, or beat an old robe-cloth, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
"But whoever," means whoever such as... [as before] ...
"a monk."
... [and so on] ... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
One who is unrelated (*aññātikā*) means one who is not connected through the mother's side or the father's side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
A bhikkhunī is one who has received full ordination in both Saṅghas.
An old robe means:
Even if it has been worn once or even once wrapped around,
if she washes it herself or orders it to be washed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Once washed, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
If he commands, "Dye it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When it has been dyed, it becomes subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya).
If he commands, "Beat it [with a stick]," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If a blow with the hand or a blow with a club is given even once, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
... [as before] ... "Venerable sir, this old robe-cloth of mine, which was washed by a nun who is not a relative, is to be forfeited.
I hereby forfeit it to the Saṅgha. ... [as before] ...
"Should give" means ...
"should give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."
If he has an unrelated woman wash an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If he has an unrelated woman wash and dye an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in addition to the offense involving forfeiture.
If he has an unrelated woman wash and beat an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing in addition to the offense involving forfeiture.

If he has an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, wash, dye, or beat an old robe, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) and two offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If he has an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, have an old robe dyed, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If he has an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, have an old robe dyed and beaten, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If one causes an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, to dye or wash an old robe, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) together with the forfeiture (nissaggiya).
If one causes an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, to dye, beat, and wash an old robe, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with the forfeiture for two [acts].
If one causes an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, to beat an old robe, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If a monk has an unrelated woman beat or wash an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If a monk has an unrelated woman beat or dye an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense entailing relinquishment.
If a monk has an unrelated woman beat, wash, and dye an old robe, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with two offenses entailing relinquishment.
If she is unrelated and he is in doubt … if she is unrelated and he perceives her as related … if he has another person wash an old robe, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she has someone wash a sitting mat or a rug, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she has someone wash [it] for one who is fully ordained in only one [Order], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative but perceives her as a non-relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative and he perceives her as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
While a relative woman is washing, a non-relative woman acts as her companion;
she washes without being told;
she causes [the cloth] to be washed while it has not yet been used.
If, setting aside the robe, one causes another requisite to be washed for a trainee nun or a novice nun; or...
"For one who is insane," "for a first-time offender.
The fourth training rule on old robes is finished.
